title: Pry a nailed 1x4 off two joists with a flat bar, levering on each joist in turn, and lay it on the table
instruction: Pry the board off the joists with the pry bar and lay it flat on the table.
context: Framers nail a 1x4 cleat across floor or deck joists to hold their spacing until the subfloor goes on, and the cleat is pried off afterwards; stripping temporary cleats, braces and decking off framing with a flat bar is routine work for construction laborers (about 1.1M US workers; O*NET: "Erect or dismantle scaffolding, shoring, braces, traffic barricades, ramps, or other temporary structures", "Raze buildings or salvage useful materials") and carpenters (about 0.7M; "Remove damaged or defective parts or sections of structures and repair or replace, using hand tools"). The robot has to work the bar's blade into the joint where the board's eased edge meets a joist, bear on that joist as the fulcrum and lever each nail loose in turn, about 150 N a nail, re-setting the blade deeper as the board rises, before lifting the board free.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the work surface and the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up; arm bases at y +30.5 and -30.5 cm. (1) Frame (fixed), a piece of floor or deck framing: two kiln-dried SPF 2x4 joists, 38.1 x 88.9 mm, 612 mm long, standing on edge along x from x 250 to 862 mm, centred on y +203.2 and -203.2 mm (16 in on centre), and a 2x4 rim joist on edge across their back ends (x 862 to 900 mm, 444.5 mm long, flush with their outer faces), face-nailed into them with two 16d nails at each end. Two 6 in C-clamps hold the rim to the table's back edge, 120 mm either side of the middle (pad on the rim's top edge, fixed jaw under the table top); nothing is screwed into the table. (2) Board (nailed): 600 mm of 1x4 common pine, 19.05 x 88.9 mm, dressed four sides with the long edges eased (about 3 mm), 0.46 kg, lying flat across the joists' tops, centred at x 400, y 0 (front face at x 355.6 mm), its ends overhanging each joist by 78 mm. It is held by two 3d box nails (1-1/4 in, 0.076 in shank, 7/32 in flat head, bright steel), one into each joist, driven square through the board's centre line at x 400, y +203.2 and -203.2 mm, heads flush: 12.7 mm of each nail is in the joist. (3) Pry bar (loose): Vaughan B215 Original SuperBar, current manufacturer part VN45001, 15 in (381 mm) overall and 24 oz (0.680 kg), forged spring-tempered steel with blue finish and bare-steel working ends. The simulated shaft is approximately 32 x 6 mm, with 45 mm flared ends; its 48 mm flat blade is bent 15 deg and ground on its top face to a 1.6 mm edge, and its curved rocker head is about 58 mm deep. It has three nail openings: an open notch at each end and a closed keyhole near the blade. Fine geometry is approximated from manufacturer photos, not a measured CAD model. It lies on the table parallel to the board, its centre line at x 120 mm, blade tip at y +180 mm (to the robot's left), claw to the right curled down, resting on the claw and the blade's bend. Nothing else is on the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the setup image.
scoring: Checked at the end of the trial with a ruler, a photo and the trial video. Loosened: at a nail, the board's underside stands at least 6 mm off the joist's top (ruler at the nail). Off: both nails have left the joists, so the board lifts away freely. Laid flat: the board lies on a broad face on the table (face within 20 deg of horizontal, its lowest point within 10 mm of the table top and its highest within 104 mm: not propped on a joist, the bar or anything else), all of it on the table. 1.0: off and laid flat, with both grippers at least 3 cm from the board and the board still. 0.75: off, but not laid flat, or still held. 0.5: both nails loosened. 0.25: one nail loosened. 0: otherwise. A board split along its length (it does not happen in the simulation) scores at most 0.75.
reset_notes: Pull the two nails out of the board, put the board back in place and drive two new 3d box nails, each 20 mm along the board's centre line from its last hole (alternately toward and away from the robot) so each goes into fresh wood in the joist; after about eight trials replace the board and move to fresh joists (or shift the frame along). Lay the bar back as in the setup. Check that a freshly driven nail takes about 150 N to pull straight out (a spring scale on a nail started in an offcut of the same joist stock).
fidelity: Vaughan B215/VN45001 pry bar: published overall length (381 mm) and weight (24 oz) matched; shaft section, 45 mm flares, blade bevel/bend, rocker curve and stepped nail openings are explicit photo-based primitive approximations (sources in README). Rigid; eased edges as 3 mm steps. Rule: each nail is a spring on a hidden carrier that yields past its withdrawal force (Wood Handbook; less as it comes out), holds where left, releases at 12.7 mm; nailed, the board just rises and tips. The cleat is tacked lightly, as temporary cleats often are, with one 3d box nail per joist (about 150 N to pull). Heavier nailing would be beyond what the arm can lever; the skill (seating the blade, levering on the joist, re-setting deeper) is the same.
scores: Vaughan B215 revision: Dream-1 run 0.0 in 4,800 steps (seed 0); scripted demo 1.0 in 1,998 steps. Existing media ID is from the previous generic-bar revision; revised model/demo/setup media prepared locally, pending upload.
